lessons.title: Creativity Is a Choice, Not a Gift
lessons.key_idea: Creative work is not a talent some people are born with but a practice anyone can choose to commit to.

lessons.title: Trust the Process, Not the Outcome
lessons.key_idea: Because you cannot control how your work is received, you should commit to the process of making it rather than the result.

lessons.title: Fear Is the Real Block
lessons.key_idea: Creative block is really fear of doing bad work, and the cure is to keep producing, including work that isn't good yet.

lessons.title: Who Is It For?
lessons.key_idea: Good creative work is made for a specific audience and aims to create a specific change for them, not to please everyone.

lessons.title: Your Work Is a Generous Gift
lessons.key_idea: Sharing your work is an act of generosity, and holding it back out of fear means withholding something others might need.

lessons.title: Professionals Ship
lessons.key_idea: Professionals release their work on schedule, aiming for good enough for its purpose instead of hiding behind perfectionism.

lessons.title: Show Up and Do It Again
lessons.key_idea: The practice is an ongoing loop of showing up, making, shipping, and learning, with no finish line and no permission required.

plan.title: The Practice
plan.author: Seth Godin
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's core arguments and recurring themes well, but not its exact chapter-by-chapter structure, so the lessons focus on its central ideas rather than precise sequencing.
plan.one_liner: Creativity isn't a gift you wait for. It's a practice you choose, show up for, and ship.
plan.summary: Seth Godin argues that creative work is not reserved for a lucky few with special talent. It is a practice anyone can choose: a habit of showing up, doing the work, and sharing it, regardless of how it is received. He urges readers to trust the process rather than obsess over outcomes they cannot control. Godin treats fear, not lack of ideas, as the real obstacle behind blocks and perfectionism. He insists that good work is made for someone specific, to change something for them, which makes it an act of generosity. Professionals, in his view, ship on schedule, accept that their work is good enough for its purpose, and then do it again. The book is a short, encouraging push to stop waiting for permission and start making things that matter.
